Sympathetic neuron: AP transmission soma → axon → varicosity

neuron/sympathetic (soma sympathetic, axon sympathetic_monolithic_v01, varicosity sympathetic). Simulation only, no module file changed. Built by tools/neuron_ap_transmission.py; CVODE (myokit), rtol 1e-8, 1 s, output every 0.01 ms; stimulus I_in_mod_soma_membrane from t = 0. The check is the neuron spec's invariants: equal spike counts (upward 0 mV crossings, at least one) and axon peak within 20 mV of the soma peak.

Recommendation

Smallest change that passes: shorten the lumped axon, L_ax_axon 318 → 106 um (L/3), keeping d_ax, R_i, channel_ratio. This is a single definitional parameter. It gives R 100 MOhm and C 3.3 pF, so tau_eff = RC/(1+channel_ratio) falls from 2.0 ms to 0.22 ms. At 50 pA the varicosity peaks at 42.6 mV against the soma's 55.8 mV, with a soma→varicosity delay of 0.14 ms. Spike counts match at every current, and the soma's spike counts are the isolated soma's. NE release goes from 0.619 to 1.385 uM peak. Use L/4 (80 um) if you want the varicosity closer to the soma: L/4 is within 6 mV, L/3 within 14 mV. The first-spike latency at 50 pA is 24.3 ms (L/3) against 22.3 ms isolated and 28.0 ms now, because the shorter axon loads the soma less.

The axon's length is no longer an anatomical length then. It becomes the electrotonic length of one lumped compartment, which is honest for a single-node "pass the AP on" axon. channel_ratio ~10 passes too (39.4 mV), but it has no physical meaning at that size: it scales the axial current by 11 on the axon side only, so charge is not conserved. R_i/10 (7.4 ohm cm) passes but is far below any axoplasm value, and d_ax only passes near d ~ 8 um, where C (80 pF) is far larger than the soma's own and the soma's AP shrinks (47 mV at d 5 um). The HH prototype passes the check, but its axon fires first and drives the soma, and at 22 degC kinetics it oscillates: see option 3.

Why it attenuates

  • The varicosity is no load. SN_varicosity_membrane is a pass-through: V = V_in (the axon's V). Its ionic currents (i_CaN, i_NaCa) drive Ca only and never feed back on V. So the axon node is the varicosity; the two traces are identical. A real varicosity of d 1.24 um (A 4.84 um2) would add only 0.05 pF against the axon's 10 pF, so its load is negligible either way (option 4: nothing to fix).
  • The axon is a first-order low-pass with unit DC gain. The node has no membrane leak and its far end is sealed. All the axial current I = (V_soma − V)/R charges the node's own capacitance, scaled by (1 + channel_ratio): dV/dt = (1 + cr) (V_soma − V)/(R C). That is an RC filter with tau_eff = R C/(1 + cr) = 300 MOhm × 10 pF / 1.5 = 2.0 ms.
  • The AP is shorter than tau_eff. The fast part of the somatic spike (above +25 mV) lasts only 0.76 ms; the trace is above 0 mV for 1.74 ms, mostly on a slow shoulder near 0 mV (half-amplitude width 2.07 ms). The node charges for less than one time constant, reaches only about -6 mV (roughly 1 − exp(−w/tau) of the ~125 mV swing) and never crosses 0 mV. The sweep below shows that every single-compartment change (R_i, L_ax, d_ax, channel_ratio) falls on one curve of tau_eff. The check needs tau_eff below about 0.3 ms.
  • Load on the soma. The axon is a series R–C (300 MOhm, C/(1+cr) = 6.7 pF) hung on the soma's 30 pF. During the AP it draws up to 0.31 nA, about 6 times the 50 pA stimulus, but only for the AP's duration. It delays the first spike (28.0 vs 22.3 ms isolated at 50 pA), but it does not cause the single spike: the isolated soma also fires once in 1 s at 20, 50 and 100 pA (and 6 times at 200 pA, the same as in the neuron). So "the axon drains the soma" is not borne out in this library. The neuron's single spike at 100 pA is the soma's own behaviour (its M/SK adaptation), which belongs to the soma review.
  • Why the "+1.5" does not help: channel_ratio only shortens tau_eff by 1/(1+cr). A first-order lag can never overshoot its input, so no linear passive node gives a regenerated AP. It can at most follow the soma closely when tau_eff << AP width. A negative channel_ratio slows it further (cr < −1 would make it unstable).

Axon minus soma peak at 50 pA against tau_eff for each parameter family (one model, runtime parameters). The families overlap: tau_eff is the only thing that matters. d_ax gives tau ~ 1/d but raises C, so the soma peak drops (d x 5: soma 47 mV).

Option 5 estimate: a passive N-node ladder with the same total R and C, driven by the recorded somatic AP (one-way, no load on the soma). Splitting helps (the distal mode is 4RC/pi^2): 16 nodes reach about +12 mV, still 44 mV short, so no passive split passes at R 300 MOhm, C 10 pF.

Notes per option

  • 1. Axial resistance. Only the product R C/(1+cr) matters. L_ax scales R and C together (tau ~ L2), so it is the most effective lever and it also lightens the soma's load. R_i alone works but needs R_i ~ 7 ohm cm, about 10 times below axoplasm (70–200 ohm cm; Major 1994 gives 170–340). d_ax alone: tau ~ 1/d but C ~ d, so the soma is loaded (peak 47 mV at d 5 um) before the axon passes.
  • 2. channel_ratio. The sign is consistent: positive values speed up the node. Passing needs channel_ratio ~ 8–10. Since I_channels = cr I is added on the axon side only (the soma loses I, not (1+cr) I), this is an unbalanced gain rather than a membrane current. It is not a physiological fix.
  • 3. Regenerative HH current (prototype, not committed). The SN_axon component in a scratch copy of the generated model got HH Na/K/leak (E_Na +50 mV, E_K −82 mV, E_L -63.8 mV for zero net current at −70 mV). With 2× squid Na density and 6.3 degC kinetics it passes the check at every current, but for the wrong reason: the axon fires first (negative delay) and its AP back-propagates into the soma and triggers it. The soma's firing changes: first spike at 8.7 ms instead of 22.3 ms at 50 pA, 744 ms instead of 297 ms at 20 pA, and 10 spikes instead of 6 at 200 pA. So it fails the "soma close to the isolated soma" criterion. At the model's 22 degC (phi 5.6) the lumped node only reaches about +8 mV with squid densities. With 3× Na it fires on its own, repetitively, at the axon's resting load: one lumped HH node coupled through 300 MOhm is an oscillator, not a cable. A proper active axon needs several compartments (see 5) and channel data for sympathetic C-fibres. That is a model change, not a fix.
  • 4. Varicosity load. None: the membrane is a pass-through. The varicosity's own geometry is reasonable for a bouton (d 1.24 um). If a capacitive varicosity were added (C = c_m A = 0.05 pF), it would change nothing at this scale.
  • 5. Several compartments. With the same total R and C, a sealed passive ladder's far end is faster than the lumped node (dominant mode 4RC/pi2 = 0.41 RC). The peak rises with N but stays more than 40 mV below the soma's:

At L/3 (R 100 MOhm, C 3.3 pF, cr 0.5) the far-end peak is 42.5 mV lumped and 52.0 mV with 16 nodes, so the lumped node is a fair stand-in once tau_eff is short. Splitting alone does not rescue a passive 318 um axon; propagation over that length needs active channels in each compartment.
